Empirical Research Plan – Conscription and Later‐Life Earnings in the Netherlands
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy  
   • Chosen method: Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Design (FRD) centred on the
     January 1, 1959 birth-date cutoff that exempted the entire 1959 cohort from
     compulsory service.  
   • Why FRD?  
     – The policy created a large, abrupt fall in the probability of service
       that is plausibly unrelated to potential earnings.  
     – Birth-date is continuous and essentially impossible to manipulate.  
     – Because some 1959-born men still volunteered and some pre-1959 men were
       exempted for other reasons, treatment assignment is “fuzzy,”
       necessitating a two-stage (IV) implementation.

2. Treatment and Control  
   • Treatment variable Servedᵢ = 1 if an individual (or, in our data, the
     monthly birth cohort share) completed compulsory military service; 0
     otherwise.  
   • Instrument Postᵢ = 1 if date-of-birth ≥ 01-01-1959, 0 otherwise.  
   • Control group Men born in the months immediately before 1 Jan 1959.  
   • Treatment timing Service occurs at age 18–20; outcome measured in 1989/90,
     roughly 10 years after service for the cohorts at the cutoff.  
   • Running variable Rᵢ = (month-of-birth in months) – 1959m01; cutoff at
     Rᵢ = 0.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
   A1. Continuity of potential outcomes Expected earnings as a function of
       birth-date would have evolved smoothly in the absence of the policy
       shock. Plausible: no concurrent Dutch labour-market reforms tied
       exactly to birth-date.  
   A2. No sorting/manipulation around cutoff Parents cannot select a child’s
       month of birth twelve years earlier in anticipation of 1959 rules. Very
       plausible.  
   A3. First-stage relevance Probability of conscription drops sharply at the
       cutoff (≈ 30 pp). Documentable with Defence data.  
   A4. Monotonicity Being born after the cutoff never increases the likelihood
       of serving. Plausible given blanket exemption.  
   A5. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA) One man’s service status does not
       directly alter another’s future earnings within the narrow window.
       Reasonable at cohort-month level.

4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  
   1. Age/experience differences: A 1959-born man is one year younger than a
      1958-born man in 1989.  
      → Use very narrow bandwidths (±24 or ±12 months) so the maximum age gap
        is one or two years; include polynomial controls in running variable;
        replicate in 1990 earnings where the gap narrows further.  
   2. Other cohort-specific shocks (e.g., university expansion, macro cycle).  
      → Placebo tests on cohorts ±5 years away; check for discontinuities in
        observable cohort characteristics (share in education, cohort size).  
   3. Heteroskedasticity / aggregated data issues.  
      → Weight by cohort size; use robust HC2/cluster-by-running-variable
        standard errors; perform randomization-inference with cluster
        permutations across months.

5. R Code Outline  (executable)  
```r
################################################################################
# 0. Packages
library(dplyr);   library(fixest);   library(rdrobust);   library(readr)

# 1. Data Loading ----------------------------------------------------------------
coh <- read_csv("cohort_data.csv")     # user-supplied file

# 2. Variable Construction -------------------------------------------------------
coh <- coh %>% 
  mutate(dob              = as.Date(dob),                       # yyyy-mm-01
         months_from_cut  = as.numeric((year(dob) - 1959)*12 + 
                                        (month(dob) - 1)),
         post59           = ifelse(months_from_cut >= 0, 1, 0),
         mean_earn_89k    = mean_earn_1989/1000,    # in thousands of guilders
         mean_earn_90k    = mean_earn_1990/1000)

# 3. Choose a bandwidth (e.g. ±24 months) ---------------------------------------
bw <- 24
rd_sample <- coh %>% filter(abs(months_from_cut) <= bw)

# 4. First-stage check -----------------------------------------------------------
feols(share_served ~ post59 + poly(months_from_cut,2), 
      data = rd_sample, weights = ~cohort_size) %>% summary()

# 5. Main FRD 2SLS estimate ------------------------------------------------------
iv_main <- feols(mean_earn_89k ~ poly(months_from_cut,2) | 
                 share_served ~ post59,
                 data = rd_sample,
                 weights = ~cohort_size,
                 vcov = ~months_from_cut)   # cluster by running var
summary(iv_main)

# 6. Robustness: different bandwidth & outcome year -----------------------------
for(b in c(12,18,30)){
  tmp <- coh %>% filter(abs(months_from_cut) <= b)
  cat("\nBandwidth:", b, "months\n")
  print(summary(
    feols(mean_earn_90k ~ poly(months_from_cut,2) | share_served ~ post59,
          data = tmp, weights = ~cohort_size, vcov = ~months_from_cut)))
}

# 7. Covariate balance placebo ---------------------------------------------------
feols(prop_special_exempt ~ post59 + poly(months_from_cut,2),
      data = rd_sample, weights = ~cohort_size, vcov = ~months_from_cut) %>% summary()
```

6. Expected Results  
   Theory is ambiguous (discipline & training vs. foregone labour-market
   experience). For a Western European setting with short 14-month service
   spells, most prior studies find 0 – –5 percent effects. I expect a small
   negative impact: roughly −2 % of annual earnings ten years after service
   (≈ –500 guilders on a 25 k-guilder mean).

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  
   C1: Discrete, known cutoff & forcing variable clearly defined …………………. 1  
   C2: No manipulation of forcing variable …………………………………………. 1  
   C3: Strong first stage (discontinuity in treatment probability) …………… 1  
   C4: Continuity of other determinants at cutoff ………………………………. 0.5  
   C5: Appropriate bandwidth choice & robust inference ……………………… 1  
   Total = 4.5 / 5  

The proposed fuzzy RD, supplemented with placebo and bandwidth tests, should
deliver a credible causal estimate of the long-run earnings effect of Dutch
conscription.
